text: Another error is an impatience of doubt, and haste to assertion without due and mature suspension of judgment.  For the two ways of contemplation are not unlike the two ways of action commonly spoken of by the ancients: the one plain and smooth in the beginning, and in the end impassable; the other rough and troublesome in the entrance, but after a while fair and even.  So it is in contemplation: if a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.
locator: Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning (1605), Book I, v, 8.

text: Doubt, of whatever kind, can be ended by Action alone.
locator: Thomas Carlyle, Past and Present (London: Chapman and Hall, 1843), Book III, Ch. XI, p. 170.

text: Nothing in education is so astonishing as the amount of ignorance it accumulates in the form of inert facts.
locator: Henry Adams, The Education of Henry Adams

text: Vile deeds are vile, no matter whether we know or do not know what, after death, will be the fate of the doer.
locator: Felix Adler, Life and Destiny (1913), Section 9 : Ethical Outlook

text: The condition of all progress is experience. We go wrong a thousand times before we find the right path.
locator: Felix Adler, Life and Destiny (1913), Section 8 : Suffering and Consolation

text: Scarcely two hundred years back can Fame recollect articulately at all; and there she but maunders and mumbles.
locator: Thomas Carlyle, Past and Present, Chapter XVII.

text: His heart was as great as the world, but there was no room in it to hold the memory of a wrong.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Greatness

text: Fortune turns all things to the advantage of those on whom she smiles.
locator: François de La Rochefoucauld, Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1678), Maxim No. 60.

text: Friendships begin with liking or gratitude—roots that can be pulled up.
locator: George Eliot, Daniel Deronda (1876), Book IV, Chapter XXXII.

text: Good deeds remain good, no matter whether we know how the world was made or not.
locator: Felix Adler, Life and Destiny (1913), Section 9 : Ethical Outlook

text: If goodness has causes, it is not goodness; if it has effects, a reward, it is not goodness either.  So goodness is outside the chain of cause and effect.
locator: Leo Tolstoy, Levin in Anna Karenina, C. Garnett, trans. (New York: 2003), Part 8, Chapter 12, p. 735

text: In the long-run every Government is the exact symbol of its People, with their wisdom and unwisdom; we have to say, Like People like Government.
locator: Thomas Carlyle, Past and Present, ed. Richard D. Altick, book 4, chapter 4, p. 267 (1965). First published in 1843

text: Man's Unhappiness, as I construe, comes of his Greatness; it is because there is an Infinite in him, which with all his cunning he cannot quite bury under the Finite.
locator: Thomas Carlyle, Sartor Resartus, The Everlasting Yea, Book II, Chapter IX

text: Happiness is the only sanction of life; where happiness fails, existence remains a mad and lamentable experiment.
locator: George Santayana in The Life of Reason (1905), Vol. I, Reason in Common Sense.

text: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.
locator: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery (1901) Ch. XI.

text: I reckon being ill as one of the great pleasures of life, provided one is not too ill and is not obliged to work till one is better.
locator: Samuel Butler, The Way of All Flesh (1903)

text: Each man is a hero and an oracle to somebody, and to that person whatever he says has an enhanced value.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Quotation and Originality.

text: No honest historian can take part with--or against--the forces he has to study. To him even the extinction of the human race should be merely a fact to be grouped with other vital statistics.
locator: Henry Adams, The Education of Henry Adams (1907), Chapter XXX

text: Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
locator: George Santayana, The Life of Reason (1905)

text: The very ink with which all history is written is merely fluid prejudice.
locator: Mark Twain, Following the Equator, Part 7.

text: Human history becomes more and more a race between education and catastrophe.
locator: H. G. Wells, The Outline of History (1921), vol. 2, chapter 41, p. 594.

text: Now, with a rush of old memories, how clearly it stood up before him, in the darkness! Shabby indeed, and small and poorly furnished, and yet his, the home he had made for himself, the home he had been so happy to get back to after his day's work. And the home had been happy with him, too, evidently, and was missing him, and wanted him back, and was telling him so, through his nose, sorrowfully, reproachfully, but with no bitterness or anger; only with plaintive reminder that it was there, and wanted him.
locator: Kenneth Grahame, The Wind in the Willows (1908).

text: Friends, if we be honest with ourselves, we shall be honest with each other.
locator: George MacDonald, The Marquis of Lossie, Chapter LXXI.

text: Life and hope for the world are to be found only in the deeds of love.
locator: Bertrand Russell, Political Ideals (1917), Chapter V: National Independence and Internationalism

text: A truly refined mind will seem to be ignorant of the existence of anything that is not perfectly proper, placid, and pleasant.
locator: Charles Dickens, Little Dorrit, Ch. 5 - Something Wrong Somewhere (1855-1857).

text: I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square.
locator: Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest, Act I, spoken by Lady Bracknell (1895).

text: Only an inventor knows how to borrow, and every man is or should be an inventor.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), "Quotation and Originality".

text: Jealousy is never satisfied with anything short of an omniscience that would detect the subtlest fold of the heart.
locator: George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860), Book VI, Chapter X.

text: We judge others according to results; how else?—not knowing the process by which results are arrived at.
locator: George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860), Book VII, Chapter II; in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 411-12.

text: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.
locator: Bertrand Russell (1925) What I Believe.

text: Sooner or later that which is now life shall be poetry, and every fair and manly trait shall add a richer strain to the song.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Poetry and Imagination.

text: London, that great cesspool into which all the loungers and idlers of the Empire are irresistibly drained.
locator: Arthur Conan Doyle A Study in Scarlet, Part 1. Ch. 1. (1887). As stated by Dr. Watson.

text: "It's just the same story as a doctor once told me," observed the elder. "He was a man getting on in years, and undoubtedly clever. He spoke as frankly as you, though in jest, in bitter jest. 'I love humanity,' he said, 'but I wonder at myself. The more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular. In my dreams,' he said, 'I have often come to making enthusiastic schemes for the service of humanity, and perhaps I might actually have faced crucifixion if it had been suddenly necessary; and yet I am incapable of living in the same room with any one for two days together, as I know by experience. As soon as any one is near me, his personality disturbs my self-complacency and restricts my freedom. In twenty-four hours I begin to hate the best of men: one because he's too long over his dinner; another because he has a cold and keeps on blowing his nose. I become hostile to people the moment they come close to me. But it has always happened that the more I detest men individually the more ardent becomes my love for humanity.'"
locator: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1879–1880), Book II, ch. 4 (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Love is a simple thing and a deep thing: it is an act of life and not an illusion. Art is an illusion.
locator: George Bernard Shaw, Back to Methuselah (1921), Acis, in Pt. V

text: Life is not so short but that there is always time enough for courtesy.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876).

text: Good manners are made up of petty sacrifices.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), page 104.

text: A husband is what is left of a lover, after the nerve has been extracted.
locator: Helen Rowland, A Guide to Men (1922).

text: An unhappy gentleman, resolving to wed nothing short of perfection, keeps his heart and hand till both get so old and withered that no tolerable woman will accept them.
locator: Nathaniel Hawthorne, Mosses from an Old Manse.

text: To disbelieve in marriage is easy: to love a married woman is easy; but to betray a comrade, to be disloyal to a host, to break the covenant of bread and salt, is impossible.
locator: Bernard Shaw, Getting Married.

text: A man is perhaps ungrateful, but often less chargeable with ingratitude than his benefactor is.
locator: François de La Rochefoucauld Reflections; or Sentences and Moral Maxims (1665–1678) maxim 95.

text: More helpful than all wisdom is one draught of simple human pity that will not forsake us.
locator: George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860), Book VII, Ch. I.

text: Piety to mankind must be three-fourths pity.
locator: George Santayana, The Life of Reason, Vol. III: Reason and Religion (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1905), Ch. X: "Piety", p. 189.

text: To love with the spirit is to pity, and he who pities most loves most.
locator: Miguel de Unamuno, The Tragic Sense of Life (1912), Ch. VII. (London: Macmillan, 1921, p. 136)

text: Silence is the element in which great things fashion themselves together; that at length they may emerge, full-formed and majestic, into the daylight of Life, which they are thenceforth to rule.
locator: Thomas Carlyle, Sartor Resartus (1833–1834), Book III, chapter 3.

text: Plato defined a slave as one who accepts from another the purposes which control his conduct. This condition obtains even where there is no slavery in the legal sense. It is found wherever men are engaged in activity which is socially serviceable, but whose service they do not understand and have no personal interest in.
locator: John Dewey, in Democracy and Education (1916), Section 7: The Democratic Conception in Education

text: Perfect solitude is when, for a whole day, no human eye has beheld your face.
locator: Berthold Auerbach, On the Heights (1865), trans. Simon Adler Stern. New York: Henry Holt and Company, 1907, p. 622

text: This is to be alone; this, this is solitude!
locator: Lord Byron, Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto II (1812), Stanza 26

text: The vanity of others is only counter to our taste when it is counter to our vanity.
locator: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil (1886), Chapter IV, Aphorism 176.

text: It is often said that men are ruled by their imaginations; but it would be truer to say they are governed by the weakness of their imaginations.
locator: Walter Bagehot, The English Constitution (London: Chapman and Hall, 1867), Essay No. III "The Monarchy", p. 57.

text: Truth is the most valuable thing we have. Let us economize it.
locator: Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897), chapter 7

text: The nobler the truth or sentiment, the less imports the question of authorship.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Quotation and Originality.

text: Words realize nothing, vivify nothing to you, unless you have suffered in your own person the thing which the words try to describe.
locator: Mark Twain A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889) Ch. 28.

text: High Air-castles are cunningly built of Words, the Words well bedded also in good Logic-mortar; wherein, however, no Knowledge will come to lodge.
locator: Thomas Carlyle, Sartor Resartus, Book I, Chapter VIII.

text: To be clever enough to get all that money, one must be stupid enough to want it.
locator: G. K. Chesterton, The Paradise of Thieves, The Wisdom of Father Brown, 1914.

text: The tendency of the casual mind is to pick out or stumble upon a sample which supports or defies its prejudices, and then to make it the representative of a whole class.
locator: Walter Lippmann, Public Opinion (New York: Harcourt, Brace and Company, 1922), Ch. X: "The Detection of Stereotypes", p. 151.

text: Prudence is a rich ugly old maid courted by Incapacity.
locator: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790 - 1793).

text: That system, again, which makes virtue consist in prudence only, while it gives the highest encouragement to the habits of caution, vigilance, sobriety, and judicious moderation, seems to degrade equally both the amiable and respectable virtues, and to strip the former of all their beauty, and the latter of all their grandeur.
locator: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), chapter 4.

text: Quotation confesses inferiority.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876).

text: We are as much informed of a writer's genius by what he selects as by what he originates.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Quotation and Originality; in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 653-54.

text: Surely a pretty woman never looks prettier than when making tea.
locator: Mary Elizabeth Braddon, Lady Audley's Secret (1862), Ch. XXV.

text: Obedience is the key to every door.
locator: George MacDonald, The Marquis of Lossie (1877), Chapter LIII

text: It's easy finding reasons why other folks should be patient.
locator: George Eliot, Adam Bede (1859), Ch. 46

text: There can be no nobler cause for which to work than the peace of righteousness; and high honor is due those serene and lofty souls who with wisdom and courage, with high idealism tempered by sane facing of the actual facts of life, have striven to bring nearer the day when armed strife between nation and nation, between class and class, between man and man shall end throughout the world. Because all this is true, it is also true that there are no men more ignoble or more foolish, no men whose actions are fraught with greater possibility of mischief to their country and to mankind, than those who exalt unrighteous peace as better than righteous war.
locator: Theodore Roosevelt, Theodore Roosevelt, An Autobiography (1913)

text: If we encountered a man of rare intellect, we should ask him what books he read.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (1876), Quotation and Originality.
